\chapter{Four Things You Buy --- Cheese, Egg, Apple, Money}
\label{ch:la-compra}
\hlchaptermodality{280}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name cheese, an egg, an apple and money in Spanish, and say which of them is named after a Roman gardener and which after a Roman coin.}

Complete ES-C280-dinero: name the four, then say which two carry a proper name and a coin inside them.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el queso]{el queso — the same word as cheese, honestly}

\label{lesson:ES-C280-queso}



\begin{quote}
Four things you might buy. The first of them looks nothing like its English translation, and is nevertheless the identical word.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la comida — food, and the meal.
  \item el pan — bread, which you already have.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{KE-so}. The \emph{qu-} before \emph{e} is a plain hard \emph{k}; the \emph{u} is written but never said. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el queso} — \textquotedblleft{}the cheese.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{caseus}. Spanish inherited it and wore it down to \emph{queso}.

Now consider English. \textbf{Cheese} is \emph{caseus} as well. Germanic speakers along the Roman frontier took the word — with the thing, which the Romans were better at — some time before the year 500, and it went through the Germanic sound changes until \emph{caseus} had become Old English \emph{cyse}. German did the same and got \emph{Käse}.

So \emph{queso} and \emph{cheese} are one Latin noun that spent fifteen centuries in two different mouths. They no longer share a single sound in the same position, and they are still the same word. \textbf{Casein}, the protein, is the modern loan, taken straight from the book and untouched.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Resemblance is a poor guide to relatedness, in both directions.

\emph{Queso} and \emph{cheese} look unrelated and are the same word. Meanwhile Spanish is full of words that look reassuringly like an English one and mean something else entirely — you have already met a few of those. Sound alone decides nothing; the history has to be traced.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el queso}, with a silent \emph{u}
  \item the Latin word behind both languages (\emph{caseus})
  \item \emph{el pan y el queso}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Are \emph{queso} and \emph{cheese} related? (They are the same Latin word, \emph{caseus}.) Which one is the loan and which the inheritance? (English borrowed it; Spanish inherited it.) Is the \emph{u} in \emph{queso} pronounced? (No.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el huevo]{el huevo — a letter put there for the reader}

\label{lesson:ES-C280-huevo}



\begin{quote}
A short word with a letter in front of it that does nothing at all — and the reason it is there is one of the more human facts in Spanish spelling.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el queso — the cheese, from \emph{caseus}.
  \item f $\to$ h — the other place an \emph{h} turns up unpronounced.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{WE-bo}. The \emph{h} is silent, the \emph{ue} is one glide, and the \emph{v} is that soft lips-barely-touching sound again. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el huevo} — \textquotedblleft{}the egg.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{ovum}, with the stressed \emph{o} opening into \emph{ue} — the change you already know from \emph{puerta}. That gives \emph{uevo}, which is exactly what the word sounds like.

So where did the \emph{h} come from? Not from Latin, and not from the sound. It came from scribes. In medieval handwriting \emph{u} and \emph{v} were the same letter, so a word beginning \emph{ue-} could be read as \emph{ve-} by anyone in a hurry. Putting a silent \emph{h} in front made the following letter unmistakably a vowel. The \emph{h} of \emph{huevo} is a reading aid, frozen into the spelling centuries after the fact.

English took \emph{ovum} straight from Latin and left the sense alone: \textbf{oval}, \textbf{ovary}, \textbf{ovulate}. English \textbf{egg} itself is Norse, and it displaced the older native \emph{ey} — one more everyday word the Vikings left behind.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Not every letter in a word records a sound. Some record a problem somebody had while reading.

That is a useful thing to hold on to, because it stops silent letters from looking like arbitrary cruelty. \emph{Huevo}, \emph{hueso}, \emph{huerto} — the \emph{h} appears before \emph{ue} right across the language, always for the same reason, and once you know the reason you can predict it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el huevo}, starting on the \emph{w} sound
  \item the Latin word (\emph{ovum}) and the change that gave \emph{ue}
  \item why the \emph{h} is written
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does the \emph{h} of \emph{huevo} come from Latin? (No.) What is it doing there? (Marking the \emph{u} as a vowel, for readers of handwriting.) Which Latin word is underneath? (\emph{Ovum}, the source of English \emph{oval}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la manzana]{la manzana — a variety name that ate the fruit}

\label{lesson:ES-C280-manzana}



\begin{quote}
This one is a person's name, worn down for two thousand years until nobody notices the person inside it any more.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item María · España · profesor — how Spanish handles proper names.
  \item el huevo — the egg, and its silent \emph{h}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{man-ZA-na}, stress in the middle. The \emph{z} is a soft \emph{th} in most of Spain and an \emph{s} almost everywhere else; both are standard. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la manzana} — \textquotedblleft{}the apple.\textquotedblright{}

Latin's general word for apple was \textbf{malum}, and Spanish did not keep it. What it kept was a variety.

Gaius Matius was a Roman of the first century before our era, a friend of Julius Caesar, and a writer on cooking and gardening. A kind of apple carried his name: \textbf{mala Mattiana}, the Matian apples. That phrase wore down — \emph{mattiana} into \emph{manzana} — and along the way the adjective swallowed the noun. The variety name became the word for the fruit, and the man vanished inside it.

English does this too, and recently enough that the joins are still obvious. A \textbf{satsuma} is named after a Japanese province, a \textbf{greengage} after Sir William Gage, a \textbf{boysenberry} after Rudolph Boysen. Give any of them another fifteen centuries of ordinary use and they will look as opaque as \emph{manzana} does.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
An ordinary word can have a proper name inside it, completely invisible.

This is worth holding because it explains a shape you will keep meeting: a word whose Latin ancestor looks like an adjective rather than a noun. \emph{Mattiana} was an adjective agreeing with \emph{mala}. The noun dropped out, the adjective stayed, and the ending it still carries is the feminine ending it needed in order to agree with a fruit that is no longer in the sentence.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la manzana}, stress in the middle
  \item whose apples they were (\emph{Matius})
  \item \emph{el queso, el huevo, la manzana}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{mala Mattiana}? (The apples of Matius, a Roman variety.) Which half of that phrase survived? (The adjective.) What was Latin's ordinary word for an apple? (\emph{Malum} — and Spanish let it go.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el dinero]{el dinero — one coin, three survivals}

\label{lesson:ES-C280-dinero}



\begin{quote}
You have just seen a person's name inside a fruit. Here is a coin inside the word for money — and this one left tracks in three languages.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item comprar — to buy, which this word makes possible.
  \item uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco — counting, for prices.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{di-NE-ro}, stress in the middle. The \emph{d} between vowels is soft, closer to the \emph{th} of English \emph{the} than to a hard \emph{d}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el dinero} — \textquotedblleft{}the money.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{denarius}, a silver coin. The name means \textquotedblleft{}by tens\textquotedblright{}: at its introduction it was reckoned as ten of the smaller bronze coins, and the coin kept the arithmetic in its name long after the exchange rate had moved.

That coin outlived its empire three separate times. Spanish turned it into \emph{dinero}, the general word for money — a particular coin generalised into all money, the same move you have just watched a particular apple make. Arabic borrowed it as \textbf{dinar}, which is still the name of the currency in several countries. And in Britain the penny was abbreviated \textbf{d} — for \emph{denarius} — right up until decimalisation in 1971, so that a price written \emph{3d} was quoting a Roman coin to a shopper who had never heard of one.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Twice in two lessons, a specific thing has become a general one: Matius's apples became all apples, and one silver coin became all money.

That widening is one of the commonest ways a word changes meaning, and it is worth watching for, because it runs the other way too. When an old text uses a word you know, ask whether it was still the narrow version. A medieval \emph{dinero} might be an actual coin in somebody's hand rather than money in the abstract.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el dinero}, with a soft \emph{d}
  \item what \emph{denarius} meant (by tens — ten of the smaller coins)
  \item the three places the coin survives (\emph{dinero}, \emph{dinar}, British \emph{d})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which Roman coin is \emph{dinero}? (The \emph{denarius}.) What did its name count? (Tens.) What did \emph{d} stand for on a British price tag? (\emph{Denarius} — the penny.)
\end{tcolorbox}
